[batch narration moved out of reading 2026-09-02] Amazon Web Services began as an internal Amazon project in July 2002, launched Simple Queue Service in 2004, then reached its modern form with S3 in March 2006 and EC2 in August 2006. It operates as a business segment of Amazon.com, Inc., a public company trading as AMZN, SEC filer CIK 0001018724, headquartered at 410 Terry Avenue North in Seattle, Washington.

As of the source date, AWS states its cloud spans 124 Availability Zones across 39 geographic regions worldwide, with 7 more Availability Zones and 2 more regions, in Saudi Arabia and Chile, announced but not yet live. Within the United States, AWS names Northern Virginia, Ohio, Northern California, and Oregon as public regions, plus two GovCloud regions serving government workloads. The registry here tracks 243 AWS facilities across seven states, California, Mississippi, Ohio, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Texas, and Virginia, with the largest concentration in Northern Virginias Loudoun, Prince William, and Fairfax counties, the corridor widely known as Data Center Alley.

Amazon has disclosed specific investment figures for Virginia: $51.9 billion in capital and operating expenditure from 2011 through 2021, an additional $35 billion planned for data center campuses through 2040, and $8.2 billion in GDP contribution over the 2011 to 2021 period. The company reported paying $334 million in business personal property taxes in 2022 and employing 8,710 people supporting Virginia data center operations in 2021. Amazon also states it has built or contracted 18 solar farms in Virginia, stated to generate enough power to serve about 276,000 homes.

These figures describe AWSs own reported investment and power posture in its largest US buildout state, not facility by facility specifications. Virginias position as AWSs most concentrated US buildout, backed by declared multi decade capital commitments and utility scale solar contracting, is a direct instance of the compute, power, and buildings link this site tracks: cloud capacity growth here is paired with explicit, dollar denominated grid and land investment rather than compute alone. This specific facility, recorded in this registry as Amazon AWS Data Center in St. Joseph County, IN, was not individually named in the operator-level research above; its operator field was blank in the source data and is corrected here to Amazon Web Services based on the facility own name, which unambiguously identifies its operator brand. This research was carried out at the operator level in an earlier phase of this project.

[batch narration moved out of reading 2026-09-02] This facility is one of several buildings that make up Amazon Web Services newly established data center campus in Madison County, Mississippi, spanning two industrial parks. The Mississippi Development Authority announced the initial investment on January 25, 2024, describing a 10 billion dollar commitment from AWS, which Governor Tate Reeves called the single largest capital investment in Mississippi history at the time, expected to create at least 1,000 high paying technology jobs and supported by Mississippi Major Economic Impact Authority funds for infrastructure, workforce training, and site preparation. Mississippi Public Broadcasting and other state and local outlets subsequently reported additional phases of investment, with cited figures growing over time, including references to 11 billion, 12 billion, and eventually a cumulative 25 billion dollar figure across the company broader Mississippi footprint in later coverage. Because these later, larger figures were reported across a sequence of separate announcements rather than confirmed together in a single AWS owned publication found during this research, they are presented here as a record of escalating public commitments rather than as one fixed, current total. This is one of AWS newest major campuses among its US facilities, still in a rapid buildout phase as of this research. AWS does not publish individual building addresses, capacities, or specifications, so this specific building construction date, square footage, and critical IT megawattage cannot be independently confirmed beyond its general location within the Madison County campus.

[batch narration moved out of reading 2026-09-02] This facility is one of many individual buildings that make up Amazon Web Services Ohio data center campus, spanning Franklin, Licking, and Union counties and centered on New Albany, a suburb of Columbus that has become one of the most significant data center economic development stories in the Midwest. Ohio hosts AWS us-east-2 cloud region. The City of New Albany own published materials, along with CoStar, DataCenterDynamics, Data Center Frontier, and local television and news outlets including 10TV and NBC4, document a series of AWS investment announcements in the area, including a 3.5 billion dollar, five building campus expansion, an earlier 7.8 billion dollar investment reported in 2023, and city and county economic development materials describing a combined multi billion dollar footprint that the City of New Albany credits with contributing 1.4 billion dollars to Licking County gross domestic product. New Albany city council approved a 30 year local tax abatement to support the continued buildout. Some buildings in this campus carry community assigned tracking codenames such as CMH50, CMH53, CMH56, CMH59, and CMH62, referencing the Columbus airport code, which data center trend tracking sites use to distinguish buildings from satellite imagery and permitting records, though these are not AWS own official building designations. AWS does not publish individual building addresses, capacities, or specifications, so this specific building construction date, square footage, and critical IT megawattage cannot be independently confirmed from any AWS owned source, even though the broader New Albany area campus and its economic impact are extensively documented in government and trade press.

[batch narration moved out of reading 2026-09-02] Amazon Web Services began as an internal Amazon project in July 2002, launched Simple Queue Service in 2004, then reached its modern form with S3 in March 2006 and EC2 in August 2006. It operates as a business segment of Amazon.com, Inc., a public company trading as AMZN, SEC filer CIK 0001018724, headquartered at 410 Terry Avenue North in Seattle, Washington.

As of the source date, AWS states its cloud spans 124 Availability Zones across 39 geographic regions worldwide, with 7 more Availability Zones and 2 more regions, in Saudi Arabia and Chile, announced but not yet live. Within the United States, AWS names Northern Virginia, Ohio, Northern California, and Oregon as public regions, plus two GovCloud regions serving government workloads. The registry here tracks 243 AWS facilities across seven states, California, Mississippi, Ohio, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Texas, and Virginia, with the largest concentration in Northern Virginias Loudoun, Prince William, and Fairfax counties, the corridor widely known as Data Center Alley.

Amazon has disclosed specific investment figures for Virginia: $51.9 billion in capital and operating expenditure from 2011 through 2021, an additional $35 billion planned for data center campuses through 2040, and $8.2 billion in GDP contribution over the 2011 to 2021 period. The company reported paying $334 million in business personal property taxes in 2022 and employing 8,710 people supporting Virginia data center operations in 2021. Amazon also states it has built or contracted 18 solar farms in Virginia, stated to generate enough power to serve about 276,000 homes.

These figures describe AWSs own reported investment and power posture in its largest US buildout state, not facility by facility specifications. Virginias position as AWSs most concentrated US buildout, backed by declared multi decade capital commitments and utility scale solar contracting, is a direct instance of the compute, power, and buildings link this site tracks: cloud capacity growth here is paired with explicit, dollar denominated grid and land investment rather than compute alone. This specific facility, recorded in this registry as Amazon in Bexar County, TX, was not individually named in the operator-level research above; its operator field was blank in the source data and is corrected here to Amazon Web Services based on the facility own name, which unambiguously identifies its operator brand. This research was carried out at the operator level in an earlier phase of this project.

reading:
Amazon Web Services began as an internal Amazon project in July 2002, launched Simple Queue Service in 2004, then reached its modern form with S3 in March 2006 and EC2 in August 2006. It operates as a business segment of Amazon.com, Inc., a public company trading as AMZN, SEC filer CIK 0001018724, headquartered at 410 Terry Avenue North in Seattle, Washington.

As of the source date, AWS states its cloud spans 124 Availability Zones across 39 geographic regions worldwide, with 7 more Availability Zones and 2 more regions, in Saudi Arabia and Chile, announced but not yet live. Within the United States, AWS names Northern Virginia, Ohio, Northern California, and Oregon as public regions, plus two GovCloud regions serving government workloads. The registry here tracks 243 AWS facilities across seven states, California, Mississippi, Ohio, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Texas, and Virginia, with the largest concentration in Northern Virginia's Loudoun, Prince William, and Fairfax counties, the corridor widely known as Data Center Alley.

Amazon has disclosed specific investment figures for Virginia: $51.9 billion in capital and operating expenditure from 2011 through 2021, an additional $35 billion planned for data center campuses through 2040, and $8.2 billion in GDP contribution over the 2011 to 2021 period. The company reported paying $334 million in business personal property taxes in 2022 and employing 8,710 people supporting Virginia data center operations in 2021. Amazon also states it has built or contracted 18 solar farms in Virginia, stated to generate enough power to serve about 276,000 homes.

These figures describe AWS's own reported investment and power posture in its largest US buildout state, not facility by facility specifications. Virginia's position as AWS's most concentrated US buildout, backed by declared multi decade capital commitments and utility scale solar contracting, is a direct instance of the compute, power, and buildings link this site tracks: cloud capacity growth here is paired with explicit, dollar denominated grid and land investment rather than compute alone.
